chapters.title: The Making of Modern Evangelicalism
chapters.subtitle: Where did the altar call, the sinner's prayer and the rapture chart come from?
chapters.nutshell: Modern evangelicalism grew out of Pietism and the revivals of the 1700s and 1800s. It gave the world a passion for Scripture, personal faith, worldwide mission, Bible translation and social reform. It also packaged the gospel in new ways — the altar call, the sinner's prayer, the rapture chart — many of which are younger than most Christians assume.
chapters.bigIdea: Evangelicalism is a real gift to the church, but many of its familiar habits are recent Western inventions, not the original shape of biblical faith.
skeleton: 1600s–1700s: Pietism and Wesley call for a living, felt faith
1730s–1840s: the Great Awakenings turn revival into a method
1790s–1900s: missions, Bible societies and the fight against slavery
1830s–1920s: dispensationalism, the rapture and fundamentalism
1900s–today: Pentecostal, charismatic, media, prosperity and mega-church movements
Weighing it: four marks, real strengths, Western blind spots

sections.h: Roots: Pietism and the warmed heart
p: By the 1600s many Protestant churches in Europe had become correct but cold. German Pietism (Philipp Jakob Spener's *Pia Desideria*, 1675) called for Bible study in small groups, holy living and a heartfelt faith. The Moravians at Herrnhut (1727) carried this spirit into prayer and mission.

In 1738 John Wesley heard Luther's preface to Romans read in a London meeting and felt his heart “strangely warmed”. Methodism followed: open-air preaching, hymns, and class meetings where believers confessed and encouraged one another weekly. This was not lonely individualism — it was strong, disciplined community.

The First Great Awakening (1730s–1740s) spread through Jonathan Edwards' preaching in New England and George Whitefield's huge open-air crowds on both sides of the Atlantic. Edwards saw revival as a surprising work of God.

The Second Great Awakening (about 1790–1840) was different. On the American frontier, camp meetings drew thousands. In the 1820s–30s Charles Finney taught that revival is “not a miracle” but the right use of means. His “new measures” included the anxious bench, where seekers came forward to be prayed for — a forerunner of the altar call. Salvation was now framed as a decision made at a meeting, which fitted the frontier ideal of the free, self-made individual.

This is evangelicalism's great strength. The 1790s and 1800s saw an explosion of voluntary societies: the Baptist Missionary Society (1792, with William Carey, who went to India), the British and Foreign Bible Society (1804), the American Bible Society (1816) and many more. Thousands of languages, Tamil among them, received Scripture, schools and hospitals.

Evangelicals such as William Wilberforce and the Clapham circle campaigned for decades until Britain abolished the slave trade (1807) and slavery in its empire (1833). Others fought child labour, cruelty and illiteracy. Any fair history must start here.

sections.h: Rapture, fundamentals and the twentieth century
p: In the 1830s John Nelson Darby, a leader of the Plymouth Brethren, taught dispensationalism: history divided into ages, Israel and the church on separate tracks, and a secret “rapture” of believers before a great tribulation. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) printed these ideas in the notes beside the text, and millions read them as if they were Scripture.

Facing Darwinism and critical scholarship, conservatives published *The Fundamentals* (1910–15) — the origin of the word “fundamentalist”. Inerrancy debates followed. After the 1940s came the neo-evangelicals, then Pentecostal and charismatic renewal, radio and television preaching, the prosperity gospel, the church-growth movement and the mega-church.

sections.h: Four marks — and some blind spots
p: A widely used historian's description says evangelicals share four marks: conversion (lives must be changed), activism (faith must be shared and lived), the Bible (the final authority) and the cross (Christ's death at the centre). All four are deeply biblical.

The blind spots are mostly about emphasis. The gospel often shrank to “get saved, go to heaven”: individual, afterlife-focused and decided in a moment. The kingdom of God on earth, Israel's story, the body, the community, and the Jewish setting of Jesus were pushed to the edges (see g-26, s-kingdom, g-07).

Three levels must be kept apart. Widely agreed history: the dates of Wesley, Finney, Darby, Scofield and *The Fundamentals*. A common scholarly interpretation: revivalism and frontier individualism shaped how salvation was presented. Debated: how far these changes distorted the gospel, and how much they simply translated it for a new culture.

Many practices people think are “just Christianity” have a birth date. Knowing that date does not make them wrong. It frees us to ask whether they carry the whole biblical story — and to keep the gold while setting aside the packaging.

chapters.title: Ten Shifts: From Hebrew Faith to Western Christianity
chapters.subtitle: How did the same Bible come to mean such different things?
chapters.nutshell: Over many centuries, key biblical ideas moved from a Hebrew, story-shaped, earthy world into a Greek, Latin and modern Western one. Salvation, sin, faith, heaven, the body, time, Scripture, church, worship and mission all shifted. None of the Western emphases is simply false — but many became narrower than the Bible.
chapters.bigIdea: Western Christianity kept the words of the Bible but often narrowed their meaning; recovering the Hebrew sense widens and deepens our faith.
skeleton: Why ideas shift: language, philosophy, law and culture
Ten shifts at a glance
Under them all: two pictures of God
Same verse, two readings
Not right versus wrong, but whole versus narrowed

p: Ideas do not stay still when they cross cultures. The Hebrew Bible was put into Greek, the New Testament was read through Greek philosophy (g-25), then expressed in Latin legal terms, then reshaped by the Reformation and the Enlightenment (e-athens, e-rome, e-reason). Each step solved real problems and also changed the emphasis.
This chapter gathers the main shifts in one place. It is a helpful generalisation, not an absolute: the New Testament itself is Greek, and many Western Christians hold the fuller biblical view.
In the Bible, salvation is God rescuing a whole people and a whole creation — body, community and land (g-26). In much Western preaching it became an individual soul escaping to heaven.

Sin in Hebrew is missing the mark, breaking relationship, and becoming defiled; the West often reduced it to legal guilt and debt (g-17). Faith, *emunah*, is faithful trust and loyalty (w-emunah); it often became agreement with correct statements.

Jesus taught us to pray that God's kingdom would come and his will be done on earth (s-kingdom). Heaven became a place far away. The body, created good and destined for resurrection (s-flesh, s-soul), was treated by Plato as the soul's prison, an idea that crept into Christian piety (g-25, g-33).
Time in the Bible is covenant history moving toward fulfilment. In the West it became either timeless eternity or detailed end-times charts.

Scripture is Israel's story fulfilled in Jesus; it was often turned into a manual of proof texts. The church was a household and a people; it became a building, an event or an institution (b-meal). Worship was the whole of life, with feasts and the shared table (b-practices); it shrank to a Sunday service.
Mission was blessing the nations and restoring creation (Gen 12:3); it became mainly saving souls out of the world.

sections.h: Underneath them all: two pictures of God
p: The deepest shift concerns God himself. The Hebrew Bible shows a covenant-keeping God who grieves, rejoices and relents (Gen 6:6; Hos 11:8). Under Greek ideas of an unmoved, passionless deity (e-athens) and Latin courtroom pictures, God often became a distant, unmoved judge. Both pictures agree God is holy and faithful; they differ on how he relates to us.

Widely agreed: the vocabulary and setting changed as the faith moved west. Common interpretation: these changes narrowed some ideas. Debated: how serious each narrowing is. The aim is not to swap one culture for another, but to let the Bible's own world set the meaning — then live it in our own culture.

Jesus taught us to pray for God's reign to come down, “on earth as it is in heaven”, not for us to escape upward.
In a Jewish household, rooms were added to the father's house for a son's new family. The image is belonging and dwelling with God, which Revelation places on a renewed earth.

cards.back: The Greek *apantēsis* often described citizens going out to meet an arriving ruler and escorting him back into the city. Many scholars read it this way: believers greet Christ and return with him.
Philippi was a Roman colony: citizens of Rome living in Macedonia, spreading Rome's rule there. Christians are heaven's colony on earth, awaiting the Saviour who will transform our bodies.
Biblical believing is trusting loyalty — *emunah* — that confesses Jesus as Lord, a title that meant allegiance in a world where Caesar claimed it.

chapters.title: Reading with Eastern Eyes
chapters.subtitle: Why does an Indian village feel closer to the Bible's world than a Western city?
chapters.nutshell: The Bible was written in Western Asia by Eastern people. Many Asian, Middle Eastern and African cultures still share its world: honour and shame, hospitality, elders, arranged marriage, oral memory, festivals, purity customs and the teacher–disciple bond. Eastern churches — Orthodox and the Church of the East, reaching Persia, India and China — also kept emphases the West often lost.
chapters.bigIdea: Eastern readers have a gift for seeing the Bible's world from the inside — if they also notice where their own culture differs from it.
skeleton: The Bible is an Asian book
Customs shared by India and the Bible
The guru–shishya and rabbi–talmid bond
Cautions: caste is not biblical purity; honour can become pride
Eastern Christianity: the Orthodox and the Church of the East
The faith in India and China from the early centuries

sections.h: The Bible is an Asian book
p: Abraham came from Mesopotamia; Jesus lived in Galilee; Paul was born in Tarsus. Every biblical writer was a Western Asian. Its first readers lived in villages of extended families, elders at the gate, guests at the door, festivals by the moon and food shared from one dish.

Many readers in India, the Middle East and Africa recognise this world at once. Things a Western reader needs explained — bowing, removing sandals, a father running to his son — feel familiar (b-life).

Honour and shame shape the stories: the prodigal's father runs and shames himself to restore his son (Luke 15:20). Hospitality is sacred (Gen 18). Marriage is arranged between families, with gifts (Gen 24). Proverbs and oral memory carry wisdom. Purity customs govern washing, food and death (Mark 7:3–4).

The bond between a teacher and a disciple is especially clear to Tamil readers. The Tamil Bible's word for disciple, சீஷன், comes from Sanskrit *śiṣya* — the student of a guru. Like a rabbi's *talmid*, the disciple lives with the teacher, serves him and copies his life, not just his words.

Similar customs do not make every custom biblical. Caste is not biblical purity: in the Bible, impurity is temporary, everyone becomes impure at times, and it is removed by washing and time, not fixed by birth. Peter learned to call no person common (Acts 10:28); in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek (Gal 3:28).
Honour can become pride. Jesus warned against seeking the best seats (Luke 14:7–11) and turned honour upside down by washing feet (John 13).

The Greek-speaking East developed differently from the Latin West (e-rome). Orthodox churches stress *theosis* — union with God, sharing in his life (2 Pet 1:4); worship as heaven on earth through the liturgy; salvation as a mystery to be lived, not only explained; and Easter as the centre: “Christ is risen, trampling down death by death.”

Many Orthodox theologians speak of “ancestral sin” — inheriting death and a wounded nature from Adam — rather than inherited guilt as in Augustine's reading of Romans 5:12 (g-39). Views vary, so this is a broad emphasis, not a rule.

sections.h: The Church of the East: Persia, India and China
p: From Pentecost, the faith spread east as well as west (Acts 2:9 names Parthians, Medes and Elamites). Edessa became an early Syriac-speaking centre; Persian churches grew under the Sasanian empire. Syriac Christians took the gospel along the trade routes.

Kerala's St Thomas Christians hold that the apostle Thomas came in AD 52 and died near Mylapore (Chennai). This is a strong tradition; early written sources are few and debated. In China, the Xi'an stele, set up in 781, records a mission arriving in 635. Christianity was Asian long before it was European.

chapters.title: Recovering the Hebraic Lens — Wisely
chapters.subtitle: How can we read with both eyes without falling off the other side of the road?
chapters.nutshell: The West gave the church real gifts: careful reading, translation, universities, hospitals, science, human rights and worldwide mission. Recovering the Bible's Hebrew world should add to these, not throw them away. It also has dangers: legalism, pride, myths and false etymologies, rejecting the Greek New Testament, and both antisemitism and romanticising.
chapters.bigIdea: Read with both eyes: let the Bible's Hebrew world shape the meaning, keep the West's gifts, and avoid the extremes on both sides.
skeleton: What the West rightly gave
Reading with both eyes
Six steps for any passage
Practices that recover the lens
Warnings against overcorrection
Read, understand, live, share

p: It would be ungrateful and untrue to blame the West for everything. Western Christians preserved and copied manuscripts, built universities and hospitals, developed careful grammar and textual study, encouraged modern science, argued for human dignity and rights, and carried the gospel and the Bible to almost every language — including Tamil (t-translation).
Even the tools used to recover the Hebrew background — lexicons, archaeology, the study of the Dead Sea Scrolls — are largely gifts of Western scholarship.

One eye looks at the Bible's own world: Hebrew words, Jewish customs, the covenant story. The other eye uses careful reasoning, history and the church's long reflection. With one eye closed, you lose depth.

Remember that the New Testament was written in Greek by Jews already shaped by Greek culture. Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28). Hebrew and Greek are not enemies; the aim is to read each word in its real setting (e-minds).

Read whole books and stories, not single verses. Ask what a passage meant to its first hearers before asking what it means for you. Learn a few key Hebrew words (w-intro). Practise faith in community. Recover Sabbath and the feasts as rhythms of grace, not rules for salvation. Eat together. Care for bodies, families and the land as well as souls (b-practices, b-meal).

Some movements swing too far. Making Torah-observance — Sabbath, food laws, feasts — a test of salvation for Gentile believers is exactly what the apostles refused (Acts 15; Gal 2–5). Pride in being “Hebraic” can become a new elitism or an anti-Western scorn.

Popular “Hebrew roots” teaching often spreads myths and false word-meanings (d-claims, d-scribe). Some even reject the Greek New Testament as corrupted — but it is the earliest text we have. And romanticising Jews, or turning against them, both fail to love real people.

Check claims with good sources. Hold debated points lightly. Keep Jesus, not a culture, at the centre. The goal is not to become ancient Israelites or to escape the West, but to hear the Bible as its first readers did — and then live it faithfully where you are.

steps.d: Read the full story or chapter, not just the verse.
Who wrote it, to whom, when, and in what situation?
Look up the Hebrew or Greek word behind important terms, using reliable tools.
What earlier Scripture is being quoted or echoed?
What would it have meant to them, in their culture?
Apply the same meaning in your own life and community.

diagrams.title: Eight practices that recover the lens

cards.back: Read a Gospel or letter in one or two sittings, as it was first heard aloud.
cards.echo: Letters were read to whole churches

cards.back: Ask what the passage meant to its original audience before applying it to yourself.
Learn words like *shalom*, *chesed*, *emunah*, *torah* and *teshuvah* with trustworthy tools.
Read, pray and decide together; let others speak into your life.
Rest one day a week as trust in God, not as a test of salvation.
Study Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles to see Jesus in Israel's year — freely, not as law.
Meals were where Jesus welcomed, taught and forgave. Make your table a place of grace.
Serve the whole person and the community, as Jesus healed and taught.

left.label: Helpful recovery
items: Understands Jesus as a Jew in his setting
Enjoys feasts and Sabbath as gifts
Learns real Hebrew from good sources
Values the Greek New Testament
Thanks the West for its gifts
Loves Jewish people as real neighbours

right.label: Unhelpful extremes
items: Treats culture as more important than Christ
Makes Torah-keeping a test of salvation (Gal 5:4)
Spreads myths and false etymologies
Calls the Greek text corrupt
Looks down on Western Christians
Romanticises or resents Jews

nodes.d: Read whole passages slowly, often aloud and together.
Learn the setting, the words and the story they belong to.
Obey: a Hebrew kind of knowing is doing (Jas 1:22).
Teach and bless others, which sends you back to read again.

verses.text: My judgement is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God.
For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore.
They read from the book, from the Law of God, clearly, and they gave the sense.
Be doers of the word, and not hearers only.

keyPoints: The West gave the church real gifts: careful reading, translation, universities, hospitals, science and mission.
Read with both eyes: the Bible's Hebrew world and careful reasoning together.
A simple method: read the whole, find the setting, check words, hear the Old Testament, ask the first hearers, live it.
Avoid overcorrection: legalism, pride, myths, rejecting the Greek New Testament, antisemitism or romanticising.
Keep Jesus, not a culture, at the centre.
reflect: Which of the eight practices could you begin this month?
Have you met any of the “extremes”? How would you answer them gently?

quiz.q: What did the apostles decide in Acts 15 about Gentile believers?
options: They must keep the whole Torah
They should not be burdened with the Law as a condition
quiz.why: Acts 15:19 — do not trouble Gentiles who turn to God.

options: Calling the Greek New Testament corrupt
quiz.why: The Greek New Testament is the earliest text we have.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the six-step method?
quiz.why: Start with the full story or chapter.

quiz.q: Which is a real gift of Western Christianity?
quiz.why: These are lasting gifts worth keeping.

terms.def: Reading Scripture within its Hebrew and Jewish setting.
Swinging so far from one error that you fall into another.
An invented or mistaken claim about a word's origin or meaning.
Making rule-keeping the basis of being accepted by God.
Serving the whole person — body, soul, family and community.
